check.learner_instructions: Answer in one short phrase, without notes.

stimulus.prompt: How many semitones are in a perfect fifth?

page.learner_explanation: Counting semitones turns an interval from a feeling into a number you can check at the keyboard.
page.learner_explanation_short: Counting semitones turns an interval into a number you can check.
page.lesson_intent: Teach the semitone count and check recall of the two numbers.
page.section_title: Count the semitones in a major third and a perfect fifth

segments.body: Start on C, count four semitones to E, and say the interval name out loud before you play it. Every interval you name in this course is a semitone count, so this number is the unit the rest of the course measures with.
segments.heading: Count from the start note
segments.short: Start on C and count four semitones to E.

segments.body: From C, the fifth note arrives after the same four-semitone step plus three more. If you count from the wrong start note the number still adds up, which is why you say the start note and the interval together.
segments.heading: Check the count at the keyboard
segments.short: From C, the fifth note arrives after a four-semitone step.

worked_example.answer: The step is done and checked. From C, the fifth note arrives after the same four-semitone step plus three more.
worked_example.prompt: A worked example of Count the semitones in a major third and a perfect fifth
worked_example.short: The step is done and checked.

check.learner_instructions: Answer in one short phrase, without notes.

stimulus.prompt: Which interval is three semitones wide?

page.learner_explanation: The third decides whether a triad sounds major or minor, so the ear has to hear the difference before the theory helps.
page.learner_explanation_short: The third decides whether a triad sounds major or minor.
page.lesson_intent: Teach the sound difference and check the learner can name it.
page.section_title: Distinguish the two common thirds by sound

segments.body: Play C to E, then C to E flat, and hum each interval back before naming it. The two thirds are the whole difference between a major and a minor sound, so the ear is trained before the letters are.
segments.heading: Hear the two thirds
segments.short: Play C to E, then C to E flat.

segments.body: The darker, lower interval is the one whose middle note is flattened; name it before checking the keys. Naming the interval before you look at the keys keeps the ear honest; naming it after is just reading the keys.
segments.heading: Name it before you look
segments.short: The darker, lower interval is the one whose middle note is flattened.

worked_example.answer: The step is done and checked. The darker, lower interval is the one whose middle note is flattened; name it before checking the keys.
worked_example.prompt: A worked example of Distinguish the two common thirds by sound
worked_example.short: The step is done and checked.

check.learner_instructions: Answer in one short phrase, without notes.

stimulus.prompt: Which note is the third of a C minor triad?

page.learner_explanation: Both triads share the root and fifth; only the third moves, which is why the third carries the quality.
page.lesson_intent: Teach the triad recipes and check both spellings.
page.section_title: Build a major and a minor triad from a root note

segments.body: From C, stack a major third and a perfect fifth for the major triad, then lower the middle note for the minor. A triad is the chord you will find in every song analysis later, so the recipe is learned on one root first.
segments.heading: Stack both triads from one root
segments.short: From C, stack a major third and a perfect fifth.

segments.body: Both triads share the root and fifth; lowering the middle note is the whole difference. Changing the root moves the whole triad, but the third still decides the quality; build it from G to hear the same shape.
segments.heading: Lower the third, keep the fifth
segments.short: Both triads share the root and fifth.

worked_example.answer: The step is done and checked. Both triads share the root and fifth; lowering the middle note is the whole difference.
worked_example.prompt: A worked example of Build a major and a minor triad from a root note
worked_example.short: The step is done and checked.

check.learner_instructions: Answer in one short phrase, without notes.

stimulus.prompt: A song uses C, G, A minor and F. Which key is it in?

page.learner_explanation: The circle shows which chords belong together, so a song's chord list becomes a key and a set of functions.
page.learner_explanation_short: The circle shows which chords belong together.
page.lesson_intent: Teach the circle as a song-analysis tool and check one mapping.
page.section_title: Use the circle of fifths to name the chords in a pop song

segments.body: Write the song's chords, find each root on the circle, and mark the home chord before naming the key. The circle is the map from chords to a key, and the home chord is the landmark you find first on that map.
segments.heading: Find each root on the circle
segments.short: Write the song's chords and find each root on the circle.

segments.body: The home chord is the one the song resolves to; name it before the key. A song that never settles on its home chord is still analysable, because the circle still shows the neighbouring chords it borrows from.
segments.heading: Name the home chord first
segments.short: Name the home chord before the key.

worked_example.answer: The step is done and checked. The home chord is the one the song resolves to; name it before the key.
